headline: Alf emphasises that idiosyncratic, uncorrelated trades like NZD or CZK are 'worth gold' for improving portfolio Sharpe ratios
reasoning: Alf explains that the Sharpe ratio of any strategy scales with the square root of the number of independent bets. Trading only US, Europe, and Japan leaves a portfolio with very few truly independent bets and a low Sharpe ratio. Finding a good symmetric idea in an uncorrelated idiosyncratic theme — such as the NZD dual-mandate trade or the Czech koruna story — dramatically improves risk-adjusted returns. He frames this as the 'secret sauce' of sustainable strategy construction.
quote: The Sharpe ratio of any strategy scales up with the square root of the number of independent bets you have. Now, if you're trading US, Europe, and Japan, I'm sorry, but the number of independent bets you're going to be having in the book is very low. It's very low. You will have a very directional, low Sharpe ratio... If you can find a good symmetric idea in an uncorrelated idiosyncratic theme, that's worth gold literally for any allocator.

headline: Alf flags Polish zloty as the short side of a CZK/PLN pair trade, with Poland facing fiscal constraints ahead of elections
reasoning: Poland is approaching its constitutional debt limit and cannot pump significant fiscal deficits going forward, which Alf believes could slow its economy. With elections next year, this creates a negative backdrop for PLN relative to CZK. Alf frames the CZK long versus PLN short as a way to make the Czech idiosyncratic thesis even more uncorrelated to other macro positions in a portfolio.
quote: Czech versus Poland. It's a more idiosyncratic expression. Poland is on the other side of it. They have elections next year. They're hitting their constitution on that limit as well. They cannot really pump a lot of deficits going forward. This might slow down a bit their economy. If you want to make it really idiosyncratic, you go along the Czech Corona and short the Polish slotty.

headline: Japan's long-end yields are blowing out as the market punishes its weak monetary-fiscal credibility mix
reasoning: Alf notes that Japan scores poorly on his monetary-fiscal credibility index, and unlike the US has not received a structural free pass — the yen has been under attack for roughly four years and the long end of the JGB curve is exploding. He contrasts this with the US which has historically received a pass that Bessent is now seemingly trying to expand.
quote: Japan gets harassed by the market for their bad mix of monetary policy and fiscal policy. Right. I mean, the yen has been under attack for what is it like four years now. And the yield curve is exploding in the long end in Japan. And the US gets a free pass, normally structural free pass. And then best sense is no, no, I want even a bigger free pass. And then the market goes like, okay, then no free pass anymore.

headline: Alf's monetary-fiscal credibility index flags US long-end yields as 50-100bp too low relative to macro fundamentals
reasoning: Alf has built an index scoring G20 countries on monetary and fiscal credibility, incorporating core inflation versus target and whether central banks are signalling tightening. The model shows high R-squared with curve slope across most countries, but the US is an outlier — the model implies US long-end yields are 50-75bp too low. He argues the US gets a structural free pass that may be eroding under Bessent's yield-curve management attempts.
quote: Basically the index says the R square is point eight looks great, but please exclude the US because you know, these guys have a yield curve too flat by 50 to 100 basis points. Like sorry, model come again. Yeah, 50 75 basis point long and yields too low. And in this environment, you have best sense that says, Oh, no, no, they're actually too high. We should do buybacks to limit it further. And Japan gets harassed by the market for their bad mix of monetary policy and fiscal policy.

headline: Brent is a seller of all Canadian dollar tariff news, viewing it as non-credible and barely visible in economic data
reasoning: The Canada-US tariff situation keeps generating headlines but Brent argues the tariffs are not credible — they are announced, then delayed, with deadlines set far into the future (September 8th next tariff date, doubling supposedly on January 1st 2027). By that time the US administration will have moved on to other concerns. CAD had already sold off heavily and recovered on previous tariff announcements, and the economic data barely reflects the impact.
quote: Canada has been moving a lot on the tariff stuff. I'm a seller of all the tariff news at this point. It just, you can barely see it in the economic data. Sure, it's there, but I just don't feel like it's a good reason to put on a trade. Also, the tariffs aren't that credible. They go on one day and then the deadline is September 8th and then they're supposed to double on January 1st, 2027. By that time, the US administration is going to be worrying about some other thing, not about Canadian tariffs.

headline: Bessent's credibility is at absolute lows, making Treasury buyback bazooka less effective and the bond market vulnerable to hot inflation prints
reasoning: Brent draws a parallel to Hank Paulson's 2008 bazooka moment, noting that credibility is critical for such announcements to work. Bessent's credibility has deteriorated significantly — his track record at Key Square is being publicly questioned and mainstream criticism is ubiquitous. If the first Treasury buyback on or around the 9th fails to exceed expectations, it will be a disappointment. Brent flags the asymmetric risk: a hotter-than-expected core PCE print on top of skittish confidence in US policymaking could send the long end of the curve sharply higher.
quote: Besant's credibility is at the absolute lows right now... When you announce something like that, an absolute critical or crucial part of it is credibility. And I don't think that's a political statement. I think this is a pretty objective statement to say that best in credibility is at the absolute lows right now... If you're selling Dollar Yen at $1.56 and people are laughing at you on Twitter and your old boss is criticizing you in public and making you look bad... Then you come in a couple of weeks later and say, well, we're going to try the same thing in the bond market. At some point, the market just shrugs it off and doesn't care.

headline: US 30-year yields appear to be normalising relative to nominal growth rather than reflecting a structural fiscal crisis
reasoning: Brent argues that most of what is happening in the long-end bond market is an orthodox nominal growth story. A chart comparing 30-year yields to nominal growth (6.5%) makes the case that yields are simply normalising. While term premium and deficit concerns are real, they are secondary to the cyclical story. Brent cautions against getting sucked into deficit doom narratives when they have been present since 1985 without a catastrophic outcome.
quote: I would say very simplistic to say because nominal growth is six and a half percent, then 30 year threshold is your P6 and a half percent. That's a very simplistic way of looking at things. It is directionally correct though... the deficit issue is very well known. My friend Jim Bianco told me once in 1985, he was working, he was a young guy at that time. And his boss pointed to a headline that said, US becomes a net debtor for the first time ever... He turned to Jim and said, you know what, the dollar is screwed. This is the end of US hegemony. So that was 1985.

headline: Brent went long Bitcoin following the Bessent Treasury buyback announcement, citing ripe initial conditions and debasement trade re-awakening
reasoning: Brent notes that both gold and Bitcoin moved multiple standard deviations on Bessent's buyback announcement while yields barely moved, consistent with a debasement trade re-awakening. He attributes the magnitude of the move primarily to starting conditions — deeply oversold positioning and exhausted put-skew in gold — rather than the news itself being transformative. He went long Bitcoin on this thesis and the news acted as a catalyst.
quote: One of the most interesting things from the Besant day is the reaction in gold and in Bitcoin... And I did manage to go along Bitcoin after the Besant thing and more on some other reasons, but also on that reason. And what's really interesting to me about the reaction in Bitcoin and gold is... the reactions in gold and Bitcoin were like multiple standard deviations and the reaction in yields was like basically nothing. Right. So it's a super interesting situation where I think what it highlights is starting conditions being so important for things.

headline: A single hot inflation print could trigger a sharp long-end bond sell-off given current skittish sentiment around US policy credibility
reasoning: Alf argues that a core PCE print of 30bp instead of the expected 20bp would be enough to send the long end of the US curve sharply higher. The Fed under Powell is providing no forward guidance, making it impossible for the market to assume any backstop. The US is at risk of being forced to apply 'emerging market medicine' — aggressive rate hikes combined with primary deficit cuts — though the political environment makes deficit reduction implausible. His base case for resolution is either the data bails out the Fed or Bessent executes a credibly large buyback programme.
quote: What you were saying before is just the market says, oh, yeah, okay, let's go and test this at the next buyback. You show up only with 4 billion. Oh, 4 billion. Okay, we can take that. So let's go and sell a bunch of bonds. It could be, you can't predict where it comes from, but it is definitely a release valve, I would say, for macro imbalances that has been dormant for a while. And now it's definitely not dormant anymore. Right.

headline: Alf sees Czech koruna appreciation against euro and Polish zloty as an idiosyncratic long trade driven by hawkish central bank response to fiscal expansion
reasoning: Czech Republic has services inflation near 5% and a monetarist central bank governor (Michael) who is explicitly linking fiscal deficits to sticky inflation. New Prime Minister Babiš is pushing for more deficit spending, analogous to Germany's 2025 fiscal shift which strengthened the euro and pushed up Bund yields. Alf expects the Czech central bank to respond by hiking rates, making the koruna more attractive. He suggests going long CZK versus EUR for a directional positive-carry trade, or for a more idiosyncratic expression, long CZK versus Polish zloty given Poland's fiscal constraints ahead of their own elections.
quote: Czech Republic, from a macro perspective, looked for many years like a mini Germany, super low amount of public debt, very conservative monetary policy type of approach. If you remember what happened in 2025 when Germany told everyone I'm going to do fiscal deficits, is that bond deals went up and the currency became stronger. Here you have a central banker that is not going to sit there and wait. He's probably going to respond to this by hiking interest rates and make the Czech Corona more palatable... If you want to make it really idiosyncratic, you go along the Czech Corona and short the Polish slotty. If you want a bit more directional, positive care, you can do EuroCzech down, but it's a Czech story.

headline: Alf views private-sector deleveraging and public-sector re-leveraging as macro-stabilising, with inflation — not debt levels — as the real tail risk for the US
reasoning: Alf argues that every major developed-market crisis since 1990 has stemmed from excess private-sector leverage (US housing 2008, Asian corporates 1997, Eurozone real estate). Borrowing in your own currency moves risk into a controllable distribution. The only genuine macro tail risk for the US is inflation running out of control, but the second derivative of inflation is not accelerating — core inflation is elevated but stable — and the labour market is mild. He therefore cannot endorse the narrative that excessive deficit spending is leading to imminent catastrophe.
quote: Let's take a look at all the developed market crisis since 1990... they all come from excess private sector leverage, not public sector leverage... if you borrow in your own currency brand, then from a macro perspective, this problem for me is like a distribution where we're often at the, at the body of the controllable risk parameters. And the only thing that makes it go banana is inflation... Can you say that core inflation is going out of control? It's high. Is it going completely out of control? You don't have the evidence to say that.

headline: Gold call-put skew had turned negative in summer as Gulf States and central banks sold holdings, setting up the subsequent 20% rally
reasoning: Alf explains that gold's options market had seen calls lose their premium over puts as Gulf States and central banks in Poland, Philippines, and Thailand were selling gold to fund their economies. This depressed positioning and sentiment so much that very little was needed to ignite a sharp rally. Gold and silver subsequently staged approximately a 20% move. He notes this was a positioning reset rather than a fundamental shift.
quote: The gold, call to put skew had become negative again after five years or people were not overbidding gold calls over good put somewhere in summer. Basically all the Gulf States and the central banks in Poland and Philippines and Thailand were basically selling their gold holdings to fund their economies. And so this was having a big pressure down on gold and even the option market had gone no premium for gold calls at all. And so I think the level of, yeah, well, draw down and fear basically holding gold upside that evaporated positioning altogether. So it doesn't take much, right? For a volatile asset like gold or silver to stage a 20% rally, which they did.

headline: Brent recommends receiving New Zealand rates and being short NZD if the Labour Party reinstates a dual mandate after the November election
reasoning: New Zealand's Labour Party is pushing to reinstate a dual mandate for the RBNZ (abandoning the single mandate adopted in 2023). Unemployment in New Zealand is quite high, so a dual mandate would imply materially easier policy than currently priced. Brent sees this as a reason to receive NZ rates and be short NZD, with expressions like long AUD/NZD making sense on a 3-6 month horizon. He notes this is an idiosyncratic trade uncorrelated to broader macro book risk.
quote: New Zealand is talking about labor, the labor party there, this hasn't got a ton of coverage, but the labor party there wants to go back to a dual mandate, which in the sort of world of central banking is interesting because they just went to a single mandate in 2023... unemployment is quite high in New Zealand. So if you're ignoring it, then you have one policy, but if you have a dual mandate, you have a completely different policy. So to me, that's probably a reason to receive New Zealand rates and to be short the currency. If you have like a three to six month time horizon, like owning Aussie Kiwi and things like that make a lot of sense.

headline: Bessent's Treasury buyback programme is analogous to Operation Twist and could push gold to new all-time highs if executed credibly at scale
reasoning: Alf compares Bessent's buyback strategy to the 2012 Operation Twist, where the Fed bought long-end bonds and funded it via short-term issuance, which had a significant market impact. He argues that the duration absorption at the long end is what matters — $8bn in 30-year buybacks is a meaningful operation-twist-like event. However, if Bessent only delivers $4bn or signals without follow-through, the impulse for gold and Bitcoin to continue rallying would fade. He views a credible large buyback as a potential catalyst for gold new all-time highs within weeks.
quote: In 2011, the long end of the yield curve became anchored because the Fed says we're at zero. We don't care... And then they came in with this operation twist, which is nothing else than basically buying back a bunch of long end bonds and funding it via issuing short term bonds. Right. It's relatively similar to what best and as in mind, and that did have a large impact. So now question is, brand, is it just Katayama way, just blubbering about something and it will do nothing? Because if he does nothing, then the impulse for gold and Bitcoin to keep rallying is weaker, I would say. Right. If it does, then, then we're going gold, new all time highs in two weeks, I think if it does.

headline: US fiscal impulse set to fade materially from July to year-end as OBBV impact exhausts and no new major spending bill expected
reasoning: Alf argues that the OBBV (One Big Beautiful Bill) provided a significant fiscal boost to the US economy that was largely felt in June, but this impulse will dissipate between July and approximately January. There is no new reconciliation bill of meaningful size coming before the midterms, and any bipartisan spending deal is unlikely before Q1 2027. Some agricultural and military spending is in train but he views it as too small to matter at the macro level. This fiscal drag should cause some moderation in growth but not a collapse, and is one reason the Fed may be able to stay on hold.
quote: I don't see any fiscal juice in the US between July and January, the OBBV was a big fiscal juice, but it exhausted most most of its impact in June. And there is no reconciliation bill coming, at least not in decent size. There is something about agriculture and some military spending, but it's completely irrelevant for the US economy as a whole. So you're going to lose the impulse coming from OBBV between now and yeah, at least the midterms.
episode_title: On Sizing Options, The Fed and The JPY

headline: European banks up 22.5% year-to-date, with animal spirits concentrated in value and banking sectors globally
reasoning: Alf notes that while many observers are waiting for animal spirits to return to markets, they are already present — just concentrated in unloved, value-oriented sectors like European and Japanese banks rather than speculative tech or crypto. European banks are up 22.5% year-to-date as of the episode date. He argues this reflects the broader theme of accommodative monetary and fiscal policy driving 'boring' stocks higher while momentum and meme-driven trades have blown up.
quote: I was actually, as you were talking, opening my Bloomberg to check out something which is the total return years to date of European banks. There you go. So European banks are up 22 and a half percent years to date brand. So I think that animal spirits are here with us right now. They don't need to come back. They're already here. But the animal spirits are in value stocks in Japanese banks, in European banks, in that's where the animal spirits are. And I know it's very unsexy to say that, but it is what it is.
episode_title: On Sizing Options, The Fed and The JPY

headline: Alf expects the Federal Reserve to do nothing on rates for the rest of 2025, with data likely to bail out Warsh
reasoning: Alf argues that nominal growth in the US has been running at 6% and fiscal deficits at 7% of GDP, making 25bp tweaks to the fed funds rate largely irrelevant. Warsh has positioned himself as hawkish but failed to deliver rate hikes at the last two meetings, creating a credibility gap. Alf's base case is that there is no major inflationary impulse on the horizon and that growth will moderate somewhat as the OBBV fiscal impulse fades between July and January, allowing the Fed to remain on hold. He expects core inflation to settle around 3% (which he ironically calls 'the new target') and sees a broadly goldilocks scenario for the near term.
quote: My expectation is that it's pretty likely the Federal Reserve will do nothing until the end of the year. How exciting. So we might just end up in a place where it's pretty goldilocks, I think, where if I'm right, there is no inflationary impulse, growth moderates a bit... If data comes in friendly, he will be bailed out by it.
episode_title: On Sizing Options, The Fed and The JPY

headline: Retail investor participation absent from the equity rally despite strong macro tailwinds, with animal spirits dormant after multiple bubble burn experiences
reasoning: Brent observes that despite strong earnings, accommodative monetary policy, and fiscal stimulus creating ideal conditions for animal spirits, retail investors have been entirely absent from the current equity rally over the last four to five months. He attributes this to retail being burned repeatedly across multiple 'bubblettes' — Bitcoin, space stocks, quantum computing, gold, silver — and now being too cautious to re-engage. He notes this is unusual and interesting because the macro backdrop would normally support very high retail participation.
quote: Interestingly, though, in the last dip, and in the last really like four or five months, retail has not done anything that retail participation has been zero. And I find that interesting in that if you outline sort of the outlook for stocks with earnings, but also monetary stimulus and fiscal stimulus, you would think that animal spirits would be running really high... people have just lost so much money chasing all these little bubble at including gold and silver, that people now are very hesitant.
episode_title: On Sizing Options, The Fed and The JPY

headline: Equal-weight S&P 500 and median stocks making all-time highs, showing equity market resilience beneath AI-driven momentum names
reasoning: Alf argues that using the S&P 500 or NASDAQ as an equity beta proxy is misleading because those indices have become dominated by AI and momentum factors. The equal-weight S&P 500, which represents the median stock, has been making all-time highs week in and week out with no significant drawdown. This resilience reflects financial conditions that remain loose, with most central banks still behind the curve on inflation. The combination of accommodative monetary policy, fiscal deficits, and solid nominal growth underpins the broad equity market even as the AI mega-cap trade experiences volatility.
quote: I love to look at things such as the equal weight S&P 500. So it's the median stock in the S&P. And that has been trading extremely solid, right? Like you look at that, there has been never a sign of any real drawdown or anything. It's actually making all time highs pretty much week in and week out. The European stock market is trading super solid value stocks in general, banks all over the world are zooming. And so I think under the hood of this AI mania, stock market is extremely resilient.
episode_title: On Sizing Options, The Fed and The JPY

headline: US long-end bonds receiving excessive market credit relative to fiscal and monetary fundamentals; curve should be much steeper
reasoning: Alf describes a monetary and fiscal credibility index he constructed, which scatters deficit levels and central bank deviation from target against yield curve steepness across countries. For all countries except the US, the R-squared is around 0.8, suggesting markets appropriately price term premium for fiscal/monetary looseness. The US is a major outlier — it is being given far too much credit by long-end bond markets given its large deficits and persistent above-target inflation. This implies the US curve should be much steeper than it currently is, though he acknowledges short-term data would need to deteriorate meaningfully before this re-prices.
quote: If you take out the US out of it, so you can put all the countries you want in there, UK, Japan, Canada, Europe, they will scatter plot very nicely. The R square will be 0.8. So it will be pretty good. But the US completely f**** up everything in there. So the US is given them a large amount of credit by the market in the long end. And now they treat the long end of the US market. The curve should be much, much steeper given the fundamentals.
episode_title: On Sizing Options, The Fed and The JPY

headline: Brent prefers delta-1 gold exposure over options after the post-bubble burst, with a defined stop-loss
reasoning: Brent notes he was bullish on gold in June and early July but gave up on the position as it consolidated around $4,000 and failed rallies. Now that the bubble has burst, he argues the correct trade is delta-1 (buying the underlying) rather than options, because the post-bubble consolidation phase means options are poor value — implied vol has collapsed and you need a very long time for any trend to re-establish. If bullish, selling put spreads could work if done immediately after the burst, but otherwise a simple long with a stop is the preferred approach.
quote: The way to trade it, I think now, that it's burst and anything that if you're bullish something after it bursts, KOSPI would be another example now, is just Delta 1 and not doing options. Because I feel like exactly what you said, it necessitates a very long consolidation before anyone will have faith again. And so you really don't want to be buying options all the time. If anything, if you're bullish, you could sell put spreads potentially, but implied vol usually has collapsed after a bit. So if you don't do it right away, then forget about it. It's just a Delta 1 trade. You just buy gold with your stop at X and or buy silver with your stop at X or at Y, I guess.
episode_title: On Sizing Options, The Fed and The JPY

headline: Alf flags that Bessent's ESF rebalancing from euros and yen into equal weight is being linked to BOJ hiking expectations, raising questions about policy coordination

He suggests this is being interpreted by markets as part of a deal where the Bank of Japan would hike rates in exchange for this dollar-weakening action, likening it to the BOJ being treated as an emerging market central bank hiking at every meeting. He views this as a notable development in cross-border monetary and FX policy dynamics.
quote: Now we're speculating when the, whether the bank of Japan will hike in exchange for Besant, for Besant doing what? For basically reshuffling the ESF composition of yen and euro pretty much. That's what he did. Literally he has 20 billion of cash in the ESF that are not dollar. So euro and yen, and he had, I think 14 billion of euros and six billion of yen, dollar equivalent. And he basically reshuffled them back to some sort of like equal weight composition. That's all that Besant did so far, by the way. And in exchange now, the Bay of Jay supposedly hiking as if it's an emerging market central bank at every meeting.

headline: Silver and gold entering a post-bubble consolidation phase of three to six months before a potential orderly re-trend
reasoning: Alf outlines a framework for post-bubble behaviour applied specifically to silver and gold. After the parabolic run-up, the deleveraging crash, and the positioning flush, both metals have entered a low-volatility consolidation range (silver ~$55-70). Allocators have lost interest, positioning is clean, and both bulls and bears are being bled by high implied vol relative to low realised vol. Alf expects this phase to last three to six months before a more orderly trend can resume, making precious metals an area he is 'very interested in' but not yet trading aggressively.
quote: The framework I applied to this Bob Letts brand is that momentum goes up a lot. Then momentum deleverages and people get crushed. And then as you say, they basically stay away from the trade for at least a few months because it's not interesting anymore... And then at some point they'll give up and the positioning will be clean. And then we might restart a much more orderly trend again, much later, generally three to six months later. And I think that might be the case for precious metals. So that's something that I'm very interested in right now.

headline: Fed's Warsh press conference sparks bond vigilante repricing as market takes over rate-setting role from the Fed
reasoning: Brent and Alf note that the Fed under Warsh provided no intellectual framework or forward guidance at the press conference, which the bond market interpreted as the Fed abandoning its inflation-fighting credibility. The bond market responded by pushing up real yields at the long end to do the tightening work the Fed is refusing to do. Long-end forward rates in the US are now around 5.55%, compared to 4% in Japan, suggesting the market is setting a much higher terminal real rate to slow growth. The pair describe this as the 'Maradona theory of interest rates' — the Fed not touching the ball while the market dribbles the defenders.
quote: I do think brand that he's applying the Maradona theory of interest rates, which is basically like the famous goal that Maradona scored at the World Cup before I was even born. headline: Brent turning more neutral on dollar-yen, arguing the bull case is flimsy as real-money flows weaken and the spec base dominates

headline: Alf recommends buying equities — specifically equal-weight S&P 500 — as the cleanest expression of a Goldilocks US macro scenario

So I run a little back test looking back at periods where the reserve hiked once or twice maximum over a 12 month horizon. Co-inflation was a bit above target and growth was okay... And the S&P 500 returns twice its median return on a six month old in period, if you're able to get those Goldilocks conditions.

headline: Alf prefers value factor (banks, industrials) over growth within equities given hot nominal growth and central banks mildly behind the curve

headline: Brent Donnelly views June 2026 FOMC as peak hawkish; expects data to disappoint Fed hawks and rates to fall short of market pricing

quote: So my view generally has been that the June 17th FOMC will be peak hawkish because the data won't ratify the hawkishness and also worse needed to be hawkish at that meeting simply because that's what you do when you're a new Fed chair and inflation's been above target for 66 months or whatever. So the combination of worse needing to perform as a hawkish person as a new Fed chair, and then the fact that I don't think the data will ratify that means that my view is more dovish and more dovish than the market. And part of that is from oil simply because it's a really simplistic way of looking at inflation, but so much of inflation is driven by crude and gasoline that it's a reasonable way to also forecast inflation as you look at what oil did in the last three months and it's a pretty good predictor of what headline inflation is going to do.

headline: Alf sees US core inflation reverting toward ~3% annualized in a Goldilocks scenario — not runaway but persistently above target
reasoning: Alf breaks down core PCE into three components: shelter (still elevated, housing market weak), core goods (inflationary dollar/China pressure calming), and core services ex-housing (tied to labor). This combination amounts to a Goldilocks setup — not a wage-driven inflationary spiral, not a massive disinflation either.

And the bubble comes back and says, meh, I don't see inflationary pressures. I don't see major disinflationary pressures either. Like the recent boom that you have seen in core PCE annualized is probably likely to revert to the good old core PCE pressures, which by the way, are full above target. We're talking about like a 3% annualized type of level... So I look at all of this and I ask myself, where is that vicious demand driven, consumer spending driven, wage growth driven inflation runaway spiral? I don't see it. My models don't see that.

headline: Alf favours short USD versus EM high-yielders (BRL, MXN, ZAR) as a positive-carry expression of the Goldilocks/soft-landing view

headline: Brent sees short USD as a better expression of the dovish macro view, noting positioning is extended and asymmetry favours downside

headline: Alf sees buying front-end US rates as a negative-skew trade — high probability of small gain but meaningful downside if Fed hikes aggressively

headline: Brent Donnelly skeptical of Fed hiking cycle, views July hike pricing as excessive and market distribution skewed too hawkish

And it absolutely doesn't mean that he means it or that he's going to follow up in real life with real action... if you compare February 25th, of 2026 to now, Atlanta Fed GDP now is the same. Crude is up like, whatever, 3%. Unemployment rate is basically the same. Claims are higher. The only thing that really has changed, oh, and by the way, one year inflation break evens are lower now than they were before the war. But at that time, we had two cuts priced. Now we have one and a half hikes priced. So I feel like the pendulum has gone way too far.

headline: Alf frames gold, silver, Bitcoin and ARK as a single basket of non-cash-flow-generating momentum assets hurt by higher dollar carry — the 'rebasement trade'

quote: The more important point that you made, in my opinion, has to do with the momentum liquidity driven assets, gold, Bitcoin, ARK, I would put them all in one basket. And the basket is non cash flow generating momentum asset denominated in dollar... the carry on gold and silver has gotten worse on a forward basis. So you're owning an asset that carries negative gold or silver or ARK that doesn't deliver any cash flow... That narrative is very negative for Bitcoin and gold and silver, right? That narrative is very bad because these assets are a monetary protest asset. They like when monetary authorities are not doing what's necessary to keep in check fiscal authorities and credit creation.

headline: Brent Donnelly went long US 2-year Treasuries on view that hawkish Fed pricing has overshot

quote: I already went long twos because I felt more comfortable doing that. But I think you're right that the dollar has a lot of momentum. The U.S. exceptionalism trade has momentum. Yes, it's overcooked, but then, yeah, why are you fading it just at some random point? You need some kind of catalyst.

headline: Brent Donnelly is 'bush camping' waiting to sell USD, viewing current dollar strength as overcooked momentum trade
reasoning: Donnelly sees the dollar's strength as driven by rate differentials and US exceptionalism narratives but believes positioning is overdone. He notes that gold and interest rate differentials have historically told most of the story for the dollar, and both point toward the dollar being stretched. He is waiting for a catalyst — weak data, the July FOMC sounding more dovish, or a technical break — before actively selling the dollar. Corporate month-end buying has created a feedback loop reinforcing dollar strength that he expects to reverse.
quote: Right now, I'm bush camping waiting to sell dollars and buy gold. You're bush camping. I love it... I feel like I'm just kind of lurking like in Fortnite, when you're not very good at the game, you hide in the bushes and wait for people to come by and then shoot them as they walk by. It's called bush camping. Right now, I'm bush camping waiting to sell dollars and buy gold.

headline: Alf constructive on EM as long as Fed stays within body of distribution — positioning has been cleansed and carry trade remains attractive
reasoning: Alf argues that as long as the Fed hikes once or twice in response to strong nominal growth without becoming 'Bank of Brazil' hawkish, there is nothing too bad about being long emerging markets.
